A.explanation: A $0^{\circ}$ source difference would leave the $20 \text{ cm}$ path difference uncompensated, so the waves could not arrive in phase at R.

B.explanation: A $60^{\circ}$ difference is only one-sixth of a cycle and does not match the fractional part of the $20 \text{ cm}$ path difference in wavelengths.

C.explanation: A $90^{\circ}$ difference is one-quarter of a cycle, whereas the extra $20 \text{ cm}$ path is one-third of a $6.0 \text{ cm}$ wavelength beyond a whole number.

D.explanation: The $20 \text{ cm}$ extra path equals $3\frac{1}{3}$ wavelengths, giving $120^{\circ}$ extra phase shift, so the sources must differ by $120^{\circ}$ for arrival in phase.

hints: Notice the two travel distances to R are $80 \text{ cm}$ from P and $100 \text{ cm}$ from Q, so find the path difference in cm.
Compare that path difference with the given wavelength of $6.0 \text{ cm}$ to find how many whole wavelengths plus what fraction of a wavelength it contains.
Recall that one full wavelength corresponds to $360^{\circ}$ of phase, so convert only the fractional wavelength into degrees to find what the sources must compensate.
walkthrough: Identify the paths: $PR = 80 \text{ cm}$ and $QR = 100 \text{ cm}$, with wavelength $\lambda = 6.0 \text{ cm}$, and the waves arrive in phase at R.
Calculate the path difference: $\Delta x = 100 - 80 = 20 \text{ cm}$, so the wave from Q travels further.
Express this difference in wavelengths: $\Delta x / \lambda = 20 / 6.0 = 3.33... = 3 + 1/3$ wavelengths.
Convert the path difference to phase shift using $360^{\circ}$ per wavelength: $\Delta \phi = (20/6.0) \times 360^{\circ} = 1200^{\circ} = 3 \times 360^{\circ} + 120^{\circ}$.
The $3 \times 360^{\circ}$ part does not affect being in phase, but the extra $120^{\circ}$ from the $1/3$ wavelength would put the arrivals out of phase.
Therefore the waves must leave P and Q already $120^{\circ}$ out of phase so that the extra propagation phase brings them back into phase at R. This is option D.
